chunks: As for what Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Maḥbūb narrated from al-Faḍl, from Ḥammād ibn ʿĪsā, from Ḥarīz, from Muḥammad ibn Muslim, from Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, he said:
I said to him: A man blows in salat (prayer) at the place of his forehead. He said: No.

So the sound understanding of this narration is that it indicates a kind of reprehensibility, not prohibition. And it is possible that this was only disliked when it is something by which people are annoyed; that is what this indicates.

key_terms.الصَّلَاةِ: salat (prayer), the ritual act of worship in which this ruling applies
key_terms.الْكَرَاهِيَةِ: reprehensibility or dislikedness in legal context
key_terms.مَوْضِعَ جَبْهَتِهِ: the place of his forehead, meaning the spot of sajdah
key_terms.يَنْفُخُ: blows; expels air onto the place of prostration

ai.seo_question: Is blowing on the place of sajdah during salat (prayer) forbidden or merely disliked?
ai.summary: This hadith addresses blowing on the place of sajdah during salat (prayer). The wording of the report is understood as indicating karahah (reprehensibility) rather than prohibition, especially where doing so causes annoyance to others.
